Shows that 1 ha of greenhouse can yield ~365–500 tonnes, corresponding to 8–10% of Kalmar Municipality's annual vegetable needs (food_e8). Heating/lighting requires energy – link to waste heat or district heating.

food_e26.claim: A mussel farm optimised for nutrient removal in a eutrophic Danish fjord produced 60 tonnes of mussels per hectare and removed 0.6–0.9 tonnes of nitrogen and 0.03–0.04 tonnes of phosphorus per hectare per year, at a cost of 14.8 euros per kg of nitrogen.
food_e26.context: Full-scale farm in Skive Fjord (considerably saltier than Kalmar Strait). The cost was competitive with the most expensive land-based measures. Should be seen as an upper reference value; in the brackish water of the Baltic Sea, growth and nutrient removal are much lower (food_e27, food_e38).

food_e28.claim: Farming and harvesting blue mussels in the central Baltic Sea can be a cost-effective complement to land-based measures against eutrophication, despite the mussels' low nutrient content; farming technique affects the cost more than nutrient content does, and current regulations are a bottleneck.
food_e28.context: Baltic-wide study (Baltic Blue Growth researchers). Mussels from the saltier outer Baltic Sea had higher N and P content. Supports a pilot lever in Kalmar Strait, but with an uncertain cost per kg N.

food_e32.claim: Catch crops (cover crops) increase soil carbon stocks by on average 0.32 ± 0.08 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year; a new equilibrium is reached after about 155 years, with a total of about 16.7 tonnes C/ha.
food_e32.context: Meta-analysis of 139 trial plots at 37 sites (0–22 cm). Corresponds to about 1.2 tonnes CO2/ha/year. Example: if half of Kalmar Municipality's arable land (~10,000 ha) gets catch crops ≈ 3,200 tonnes C/year (≈ 12,000 tonnes CO2) – declining over time. Nitrous oxide and albedo not included.

food_e37.claim: Assumption: open-field urban growing in Kalmar (allotments, school gardens, community gardens) yields on average 2 kg/m²/year (range 1–6) and can realistically cover at most 10–25% of the municipality's vegetable needs but less than 2% of its calorie needs; heated greenhouses yield 35–50 kg/m²/year.
food_e37.context: Model assumption. Derivation: Brighton ~1 kg/m² (food_e22), Sydney 5.94 kg/m² with a lot of labour (food_e21), Swedish greenhouses 36.5–50 kg/m² (food_e24). Demand ~4,800 tonnes of vegetables/year in Kalmar Municipality (food_e8): 10 ha of open field at 2 kg/m² = 200 tonnes (~4%); 60 ha ≈ 25%; 1 ha of greenhouse ≈ 8–10%. British towns: 3–8% of fruit/vegetables today, up to 50% with maximum scale-up (food_e19–e20). Calories come from cereals, legumes, potatoes and animal products on the surrounding arable land (food_e14).

food_e38.claim: Assumption: a mussel farm in Kalmar Strait removes about 50 kg of nitrogen per hectare per year (range 25–150) at a cost on the order of 1,000–4,000 euros per kg N if the mussels are sold as feed.
food_e38.context: Model assumption. The surface water of the Baltic Proper is brackish, with lower salinity than the German trial sites west of Rostock (the exact salinity in Kalmar Strait has not been verified here), so growth is assumed to be close to the lowest part of the range in Buer et al. (food_e27: 24.7 kg N per half-year at 7 psu), far below Danish fjord values (food_e26: 600–900 kg). Should be replaced with measured data from Swedish east-coast pilots.

food_e39.claim: Sweden's national food strategy has as its overall objective a competitive food supply chain in which total food production increases while relevant national environmental objectives are achieved.
food_e39.context: The Swedish Board of Agriculture follows up the strategy annually. The goal of increased production combined with environmental objectives is the national framework for municipal and regional food strategies (Region Kalmar County has a regional food strategy, cf. food_e13). No quantitative targets for self-sufficiency were found on the page.

food_e40.claim: If all suitable flat roofs in Bologna (Italy) were used for growing, they could produce just over 12,000 tonnes of vegetables per year, corresponding to around 77% of residents' vegetable needs.
food_e40.context: Based on rooftop growing trials in Bologna, a GIS mapping of flat roofs and residents' dietary needs. The figure is a technical maximum potential and does not take into account load-bearing capacity, ownership, economics or the winter season. It also applies to a Mediterranean climate with a longer growing season than Kalmar's. The figures (>12,000 t/year, 77%) have been verified via summaries (the European Commission's 'Science for Environment Policy', according to TABLE, and search hits on the abstract). The abstract itself could not be opened. Use as an upper limit. For Kalmar the potential should be lowered sharply (assumption: at most one tenth as large a share).

food_e44.claim: Sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) requires a salinity above 23 psu for high yields and can therefore only be farmed in the westernmost parts of the Baltic Sea. Gut weed (Ulva intestinalis) and bladderwrack (Fucus vesiculosus), on the other hand, have farming potential in the southern and eastern Baltic Sea as well.
food_e44.context: Modelling of the farming potential for macroalgae across the whole Baltic Sea. The farms caused no significant nutrient depletion, and the impact spread less than 100–250 m. The spread was greater in nutrient-poor areas with little water exchange, such as the open sea of the Baltic Proper. Kalmar Strait has brackish water with far lower salinity than 23 psu (cf. food_e27, where the study's lowest salinity was 7 psu). Seaweed farming in Kalmar Strait is therefore limited to low-salinity species with lower yields. It should be modelled as a small complement to mussel farming, not as a large nutrient trap. No yield figures per hectare for Kalmar Strait have been found.

food_e45.claim: There are currently no production areas for food-grade mussels in the Baltic Sea designated by the Swedish Food Agency. In 2022–2023 Kalmar Municipality led a pilot study with sampling at sites including the Hagby mussel farm south of Kalmar. The Swedish Food Agency is positive about opening such areas along the east coast, but practical and legal issues remain.
food_e45.context: The pilot study received support from the national food strategy via the Swedish Board of Agriculture. Västervik Municipality, Vattenbrukscentrum Ost, Ecopelag and private mussel farmers took part, and Sweco was the project manager. Levels of environmental toxins and heavy metals in the mussels were relatively low. One problem area was identified near Oskarshamn. This shows that mussel farming already exists in Kalmar Strait, but that the mussels can today mainly be used as feed (cf. food_e28) rather than human food. A political choice in the game could be to push for food-grade classification, which gives a higher value per tonne and better profitability for nutrient removal.

energy_e1.claim: A solar PV system on a south-facing roof (27°) in Kalmar produces about 1,010 kWh per installed kWp per year.
energy_e1.context: PVGIS 5.3 (SARAH3 radiation database), lat 56.66 N, lon 16.36 E, 14% system losses, free-standing mounting calculation. Year-to-year variation (standard deviation) approx. 40 kWh/kWp. Range: east/west roofs with a 15° tilt give approx. 825 kWh/kWp (PVGIS 5.3), the optimal south-facing tilt of 42° gives approx. 1,050 kWh/kWp (PVGIS 5.2, SARAH2); flat roofs (0°) approx. 846 kWh/kWp. Use 950–1,000 kWh/kWp as the model value for a mixed roof stock. The figure applies to new installations; assume approx. 0.3–0.5% annual degradation (assumption, not verified here).

energy_e2.claim: Solar power generation in Kalmar is extremely seasonal: June yields about 28 times more electricity than December.
energy_e2.context: PVGIS (SARAH2), 1 kWp mounted flat in Kalmar: December 5.2 kWh, January 8.3 kWh, June 144.9 kWh, July 135.3 kWh (annual total 846 kWh). Roughly 75% of annual output comes in April–August. Key model parameter: solar power cannot cover winter electricity demand without seasonal storage, wind, biopower or imports. Batteries handle daily variation, not seasonal variation.

energy_e4.claim: At the end of 2024, Kalmar County had about 783 watts of installed solar PV capacity per inhabitant, among the seven highest counties in Sweden.
energy_e4.context: Official statistics. Starting value for the county in the model; at approx. 1,000 kWh/kWp (energy_e1) this corresponds roughly to 780 kWh of solar power per inhabitant per year. The municipal-level figure for Kalmar Municipality has not been verified.

energy_e6.claim: The Kårehamn offshore wind farm off Öland (16 turbines, 48 MW, in operation since 2013) produces about 194 GWh per year, equivalent to roughly two thirds of Öland's electricity use.
energy_e6.context: Figure from the owner RWE (2023). This gives a capacity factor of approx. 46% (194 GWh / (48 MW × 8,760 h)), which is high and typical of offshore wind. Shallow water (up to 20.5 m), 7 km from the coast. Model parameter: approx. 4 GWh per MW per year for nearshore offshore wind in Kalmar Strait/the Baltic Sea. Note that this is a company figure.

energy_e7.claim: On 4 November 2024 the Government rejected thirteen offshore wind farms in the Baltic Sea on defence grounds; according to the Government, wind farms can halve the time available to detect incoming cruise missiles, from 2 minutes to 60 seconds.
energy_e7.context: Rejected wind farms: Arkona, Aurora, Baltic Offshore Beta, Baltic Offshore Delta North, Cirrus, Dyning, Erik Segersäll, Neptunus, Pleione, Skidbladner, Skåne Havsvindpark, Södra Victoria and Triton. According to a review by the Swedish public broadcaster SVT, Aurora (between Öland and Gotland), for example, was projected at 24 TWh/year and Erik Segersäll at 19.5 TWh/year. At the same time, Poseidon (west coast, up to 5.5 TWh/year) was granted a permit. Model implication: large-scale offshore wind off Kalmar is blocked by security policy in the near term; in the game this can be an exogenous “geopolitical” parameter that may change with technology (radar compensation) or new decisions.

energy_e8.claim: The planned Kultje offshore wind farm between Öland and Gotland (approx. 220 turbines, 553 km², approx. 11 TWh/year) was opposed by the Swedish Armed Forces as early as 2022.
energy_e8.context: The Swedish Armed Forces judged that the wind farm risked “significant damage to the national interest of the military component of total defence” and, for reasons of secrecy, did not give its reasons in more detail. Illustrates the order of magnitude of the potential in the sea near Kalmar: 11 TWh corresponds to almost all of Kalmar County's total energy use (11.6 TWh, energy_e14).

energy_e12.claim: Heat pumps are three to five times more energy efficient than gas boilers, and in Sweden over 40% of buildings have a heat pump.
energy_e12.context: IEA's global heat pump report: “Heat pumps currently available on the market are three-to-five times more energy efficient than natural gas boilers” and “In Norway, 60% of buildings are equipped with heat pumps, with Sweden and Finland at over 40%”. Model parameter: a seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) of 3–4 for air-to-water and ground-source heat pumps in Kalmar's climate is reasonable (assumption based on the range). Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung (2025, with EHPA data) reports approx. 50 heat pumps per 100 households in Sweden in 2024.

energy_e13.claim: The Moskogen combined heat and power plant in Kalmar produces about 370 GWh of heat and 130 GWh of electricity each year, equivalent to roughly 90% of Kalmar's district heating demand and a third of Kalmar's electricity demand.
energy_e13.context: Kalmar Energi, consultation document 2022. Fuel mix normally 55% GROT (forest residues: branches and treetops), 30% bark, 15% wood shavings; 140,000–175,000 tonnes of biofuel per year, sourced within a radius of approx. 80 km (8 Swedish mil). Production 2017–2021: district heating 356–392 GWh, electricity 90–128 GWh. Heat storage tank of up to 1,000 MWh. Important for resilience (local fuel supply) but also for conflicts over forest biomass and biodiversity.

energy_e14.claim: Kalmar County's total energy use (electricity, heat, transport, etc.) was 11.6 TWh in 2022; the county's targets include renewable energy production in 2030 being at least as large as energy use, and biogas production of at least 400 GWh.
energy_e14.context: From Fossilbränslefri region 2030 – Handlingsprogram 2026–2028 (Fossil-fuel-free region 2030 – action programme 2026–2028; County Administrative Board/Region Kalmar County). Other 2030 targets: territorial emissions at least 80% lower than in 1990, energy use 50% more efficient than in 2005 (per unit of GRP), all energy use fossil-free. Oskarshamn 3 (nuclear reactor) produced 9.2 TWh of electricity in 2023 but counts as a national resource and is not included in the county's renewables balance. Starting value and target for the model's county scale.

energy_e15.claim: Kalmar County produced 75 GWh of biogas in 2024 at 18 plants (+18% compared with 2023); Sweden as a whole produced 2,395 GWh at 330 plants.
energy_e15.context: Official biogas statistics (Energigas Sverige on behalf of the Swedish Energy Agency). Four new farm-based plants in the county in 2024. Nationally, anaerobic digestion yielded 3.7 million tonnes of digestate (92% was used as fertiliser) – a link to food and nutrient cycles. The gap to the county's target of 400 GWh in 2030 (energy_e14) is large: a more than fivefold increase is required.

energy_e18.claim: In Kalmar, a housing company (SBF, the Safiren 2 property in Oxhagen) was granted an exemption from the grid concession requirement by the Swedish Energy Markets Inspectorate in 2023 and may build its own internal electricity grid with solar PV for 97 electricity customers.
energy_e18.context: One of the first Swedish examples of a concession-exempt grid (IKN) for local sharing of solar power; the decision came after a three-year wait (decision of 1 November 2023). Shows that energy communities are possible but the regulatory framework is slow. The industry association Energiföretagen (Swedenergy) (2025) wants everyone who uses the grid to pay grid fees and opposes tax exemption for energy sharing – a central line of conflict.

energy_e19.claim: Assumption: Kalmar Municipality's annual electricity use is in the order of 390 GWh.
energy_e19.context: Derived from Kalmar Energi's statement that Moskogen produces approx. 130 GWh of electricity, corresponding to a third of Kalmar's electricity demand (energy_e13): 3 × 130 ≈ 390 GWh. It is unclear which geographical boundary “Kalmar's electricity demand” refers to (the municipality or Kalmar Energi's grid area). Should be replaced with the municipal energy balance from Statistics Sweden (SCB) once it has been retrieved. Used to calculate the degree of self-sufficiency: e.g. 100 MWp of solar ≈ 100 GWh ≈ 25%.

energy_e20.claim: Assumption: 1 kWp of modern solar panels requires about 5 m² of roof area.
energy_e20.context: Physically derived: kWp is defined at an irradiance of 1,000 W/m²; with a module efficiency of approx. 20–22%, 4.5–5 m² of module area is needed per kWp, plus margins for edges, shading and fire access paths. Combined with energy_e1 this gives approx. 200 kWh per m² of roof area per year in Kalmar. Not directly verified against a source in this compilation – check against manufacturer data.

mobility_e1.claim: In Kalmar Municipality the car accounts for about 60% of passenger transport, while walking, cycling and public transport account for about 40%.
mobility_e1.context: Figure in Kalmar Municipality's climate city contract with Viable Cities (January 2023), from the work on the comprehensive plan and mobility strategy. The measurement method (trips or passenger-kilometres) is not stated. Starting value for the model's modal split.

mobility_e2.claim: 44% of car trips in Kalmar's urban area are shorter than five kilometres.
mobility_e2.context: Kalmar Municipality's climate city contract 2023. Short trips are the easiest to shift to walking, cycling and e-bikes. Key parameter for how much the car share can fall without major structural changes.

mobility_e3.claim: Kalmar Municipality's goal is to reverse the modal split by 2035 so that sustainable modes account for 60% and the car for 40%; the municipality is to be climate neutral by 2030 (85% lower emissions than in 1990).
mobility_e3.context: Politically adopted targets according to the climate city contract; an earlier interim target was 45% sustainable passenger transport by 2025. The climate neutrality target covers the entire geographical area, including consumption-based emissions. Used as the reference pathway in the game (“what the municipality itself has promised”).

mobility_e4.claim: In 2025, 3.8 billion trips were made in Sweden, of which about 1,946 million by car (approx. 51%), 707 million by public transport and 560 million on foot.
mobility_e4.context: Trafikanalys (Transport Analysis), Resvanor i Sverige 2025 (official statistics, ages 6–84, approx. 14,500 respondents, published 28 May 2026). Shares calculated by the compiler from the number of trips. Walking trips increased by 12% and car trips decreased by 5% compared with 2024; cycling trips decreased by 1% (the cycling share is not given in the retrieved text). National comparison for Kalmar's 60% (mobility_e1).

mobility_e7.claim: Implementing 503 superblocks in Barcelona is estimated to prevent 667 premature deaths per year, give adults an average of almost 200 days' longer life expectancy and yield an annual economic benefit of EUR 1.7 billion.
mobility_e7.context: Quantitative health impact assessment (modelling, not measured outcomes). Largest contributions: reduced NO2 (291), noise (163), heat (117), green space (60), increased physical activity (36). Approx. 51 deaths per 100,000 adults per year. Must NOT be scaled linearly to Kalmar: air pollution and noise are much lower in Kalmar, so the benefit per inhabitant will be considerably smaller and probably dominated by physical activity and greenery.

mobility_e8.claim: Since 1999, Pontevedra (Spain, approx. 84,000 inhabitants) has handed back to pedestrians approx. 80% of the street space that was allocated to motor vehicles. Motor traffic has fallen by 92% in the historic city centre, 77% in the centre and 53% in the outer district (ensanche).
mobility_e8.context: The municipality's own figures, published in the Spanish Directorate-General for Traffic's (DGT) catalogue of good practice (NIPO 128-22-050-6, approx. 2022). It also states that 66% of internal trips are made on foot, 5% by bicycle or public transport and 28% by car. Seriously injured road casualties fell from 129 in 1999 to 4 in 2020. No road deaths are reported for 12 years from 2007. The European Commission reports zero deaths in 2011–2018 (see mobility_e18). The figures have not been independently evaluated. Use them as an upper benchmark for what a consistent policy over 20 years can achieve in a city the size of Kalmar. The previously often-cited figure of 67% lower CO2 emissions could not be verified in a primary source and is not used.

mobility_e9.claim: Oslo removed 760 parking spaces in the city centre inside Ring 1 under the Car-free City Life programme (Bilfritt byliv) 2016–2023 and replaced them with seating, greenery, bicycle parking and activities.
mobility_e9.context: Oslo Municipality's programme page (accessed 2026; the programme ran 2016–2023). The programme chose to remove parking and through traffic rather than ban cars entirely; goods deliveries and parking for people with reduced mobility were retained. Quantitative effects on retail are reported in separate “Byregnskap” (city accounts) that have not been reviewed here. Useful as a sense of scale for Kvarnholmen.

mobility_e12.claim: In outer London areas where Low Traffic Neighbourhoods were introduced, car ownership and car use fell and active travel increased more than in comparison areas.
mobility_e12.context: Aldred & Goodman (2020), panel study 2016–2019 in Outer London. The small sample size in LTN areas makes the effect size uncertain, but the direction is consistent. Reduced car ownership was seen only in areas with LTNs – not from cycle lanes alone. Relevant for Kalmar's residential areas (Berga, Norrliden, Funkabo).

mobility_e13.claim: In Copenhagen, two thirds of shopping trips and half of shops' turnover come from customers who walk or cycle; retailers often overestimate how many customers arrive by car.
mobility_e13.context: Compiled in Transport for London's evidence review (2018), citing the Copenhagen Bicycle Account 2012 and O'Connor et al. 2011 respectively (retailers on two shopping streets overestimated car-borne customers and underestimated cyclists). Secondary source and contexts with a high cycling share – low certainty for Kalmar, but supports the view that a car-free centre does not automatically harm retail.

mobility_e14.claim: The “15-minute city” (Carlos Moreno, 2016) means that residents should be able to reach their everyday needs – work, shopping, healthcare, school, culture and recreation – within 15 minutes on foot or by bicycle (“chrono-urbanism”).
mobility_e14.context: A concept paper, not an impact study: the empirical evidence for the health and climate effects of 15-minute planning is still limited, and the concept has been criticised for potentially driving gentrification and for suiting rural areas less well. In Kalmar it fits the urban area and the surrounding localities (Lindsdal, Smedby, Rinkabyholm) but not the sparsely populated areas. Use as a planning indicator (share of inhabitants with services within 15 min).

mobility_e17.claim: Assumption: with strong measures (a connected cycle network, a car-free centre, e-bike subsidies, parking policy), up to half of Kalmar's car trips under 5 km could be shifted to walking, cycling or e-bikes within 10–15 years.
mobility_e17.context: Model assumption. Reasoning: 44% of car trips in the urban area are under 5 km (mobility_e2); the municipality's own target of reducing the car share from approx. 60% to 40% by 2035 (mobility_e1, mobility_e3) presupposes a shift of roughly this size; examples such as Pontevedra and Ghent (mobility_e8, mobility_e10) show that large shifts are possible, but with strong policy instruments. If half of the short car trips are shifted, the car share of all trips falls by roughly 0.6 × 0.44 × 0.5 ≈ 13 percentage points. Lower value (25%) with “carrots” only.

mobility_e18.claim: Pontevedra received the EU's first Urban Road Safety Award (2020). According to the Commission, the local police recorded no road deaths in 2011–2018, and 80% of children aged 6–12 walk to school on their own.
mobility_e18.context: The European Commission's (DG Mobility and Transport) citation, 18 May 2020. Measures included speed limits of 10–30 km/h and attractive public spaces for pedestrians. The share of children who walk to school on their own is a good indicator for the game of how independent children are and how safe the streets are. Kalmar's corresponding value is not known.

community_e3.claim: Objective social isolation increases mortality by 29% and living alone by 32%.
community_e3.context: From the same meta-analysis as community_e2: social isolation OR 1.29; living alone OR 1.32. Important for Kalmar because single-person households are common and become more common with age (community_e8). Objective isolation and subjective loneliness are different mechanisms – the model can use both.

community_e5.claim: About 664,000 people in Sweden (aged 16+) have no close friend, 7–8% of the population.
community_e5.context: Statistics Sweden (SCB) Living Conditions Surveys (ULF) 2023, confidence interval 610,000–720,000 people. Men 9.4%, women 6.1%; foreign-born 13.1% versus 6.2% for Swedish-born; less than upper secondary education 12.2% versus 5.2% for post-secondary education; 65+ 8.0%. Suitable starting value for the indicator 'has no close friend' in Kalmar 2026 (assumption: Kalmar is close to the national average; municipal-level data are lacking).

community_e8.claim: 41% of all households in Sweden consist of one person.
community_e8.context: Statistics Sweden (SCB) population statistics 2022, cited in the Public Health Agency of Sweden's loneliness mapping. The share of single-person households is higher in older age groups. Relevant for housing planning in Kalmar: an ageing population increases demand for housing types with shared spaces.

community_e10.claim: The 1995 Chicago heat wave killed 739 people in one week; mortality was roughly ten times higher in North Lawndale than in the neighbouring district of Little Village, which had similar levels of poverty but a stronger social life.
community_e10.context: Klinenberg's 'social autopsy' showed that many died alone at home and that differences in social infrastructure (shops, street life, associations, density) explained part of the differences between neighbourhoods. The figure of 40 versus 4 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants is taken from secondary summaries of the book. Klinenberg developed the concept of social infrastructure (libraries, parks, meeting places) in 'Palaces for the People' (2018). Relevant for Kalmar's climate adaptation: heat waves + older people living alone.

community_e11.claim: Restoring vacant lots (clean-up, grass, trees, fencing) reduced gun violence by 29% in poor neighbourhoods and increased the use of outdoor spaces for socialising by 76%.
community_e11.context: Cluster-randomised study in Philadelphia with 541 lots and 445 residents interviewed over 38 months. Also reduced perceived crime (−36.8%) and fear of going outside (−57.8%). A cheap, scalable 'social infrastructure' measure. Kalmar has low levels of violence, so the parameter should be used for safety and socialising in outdoor spaces rather than for violence.

community_e13.claim: The Färdknäppen cohousing building in Stockholm ('the second half of life') has 43 flats of 37–75 m² and about 400 m² of shared space, with shared dinners cooked by rotating cooking teams.
community_e13.context: Initiated in 1993 together with the municipal housing company Familjebostäder. Gives a design parameter: about 9 m² of shared space per flat. The example shows that municipal public housing can build senior cohousing – relevant for Kalmarhem. Facts from the CO-HOPE research project (TU Wien) and an architecture database.

community_e18.claim: In Gdańsk, citizens' assembly proposals with at least 80% support become binding on the city; the first assembly (about 60 people, four Saturdays), on flooding after the 2016 cloudburst, produced 16 proposals.
community_e18.context: Mayor Adamowicz committed to implementing proposals with ≥80% support. The proposals included investment in monitoring and stormwater infrastructure (nearly USD 40 million according to the article), grants to property owners for local stormwater management and an information campaign. The source is an opinion piece (grey literature). Gdańsk is a Baltic Sea city with climate risks similar to Kalmar's.

community_e21.claim: Paris allocates 5% of the city's investment budget, about EUR 100 million a year, to participatory budgeting; in 2019, 231,822 people voted.
community_e21.context: About EUR 0.5 billion over the 2014–2020 term of office. 2019: 2,084 projects submitted, 196 winners, including an earmarked share for disadvantaged neighbourhoods and one for schools. Gives a realistic order of magnitude for a municipal participatory budget; for Kalmar, the equivalent share would be applied to the municipality's investment budget.

health_e4.claim: WHO Europe proposes as an indicator that everyone should live within 300 metres in a straight line (about a 5-minute walk) of a green space of at least 0.5 hectares (alternatively 1 hectare).
health_e4.context: The report summarises evidence for improved mental health, reduced cardiovascular disease, obesity and type 2 diabetes, and better pregnancy outcomes, via stress reduction, physical activity, and reduced air pollution, noise and heat. 0.5 ha is the core indicator, 1 ha an additional indicator. Used as a target value: share of Kalmar's population within 300 m of a green space of ≥0.5 ha (the baseline for Kalmar needs to be calculated in GIS – not found).

health_e8.claim: Only about one in five Swedish schoolchildren (aged 11–15) is sufficiently physically active (at least 60 minutes a day).
health_e8.context: Skolbarns hälsovanor 2021/2022 (the Swedish part of the WHO Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study, HBSC). The next survey, 2025/2026, will be published in 2026–2027. The Public Health Agency of Sweden notes that sedentary behaviour is increasing in all age groups. Starting value for children's physical activity in the model (assumption: Kalmar ≈ national level).

health_e13.claim: Life expectancy in Kalmar Municipality in 2021–2025 is 81.8 years for men and 85.9 years for women (Kalmar County 81.5 and 85.0; Sweden as a whole 81.8 and 85.1).
health_e13.context: Statistics Sweden (SCB), remaining life expectancy at age 0, five-year period 2021–2025. Kalmar Municipality 2002–2006: men 78.3, women 82.6 – i.e. an increase of about 3.5 years for men and 3.3 years for women in just under 20 years. Starting value for the model's life expectancy indicator in 2026.

health_e14.claim: In Kalmar County, 26.3% of inhabitants are aged 65 or over and 7.9% are aged 80 or over (Sweden as a whole 20.8% and 6.1%; Kalmar Municipality 20.5% and 6.0%).
health_e14.context: Own calculation from the Statistics Sweden (SCB) population table, 31 December 2024: Kalmar County 246,352 inhabitants, of whom 64,879 are 65+ and 19,515 are 80+; Kalmar Municipality 72,704 inhabitants, of whom 14,890 are 65+ and 4,391 are 80+. Kalmar Municipality is younger than the county (a university town). Drives demand for home care, residential care homes and dementia care in the model.

health_e16.claim: 70% of Sweden's population feel they are in good health, but health inequalities between socio-economic groups are widening in several areas.
health_e16.context: The Public Health Agency of Sweden's follow-up 'Folkhälsan i Sverige – årsrapport 2025' (page updated March 2026). Starting value for the model's health indicator (assumption: Kalmar ≈ national level). The national goal is to close the avoidable health gaps within a generation.

health_e18.claim: Assumption: Every krona that Kalmar Municipality shifts from acute interventions to local preventive public health work yields about SEK 2–4 in reduced costs for the municipality, the region and the state over 10–20 years, with a delay of 5–10 years.
health_e18.context: Model assumption. Based on the median of 4.1:1 for local public health interventions (health_e12) but lowered because (1) the studies come from other countries and healthcare systems, (2) published ROI studies are probably positively selected, and (3) only part of the benefit accrues to the municipality – the region bears healthcare costs in Kalmar County. The delay reflects the fact that lifestyle changes affect morbidity only after several years.

digital_resilience_e1.claim: The state set aside SEK 685 million in 2023 and SEK 658 million in 2024 in government grants for textbooks and teachers’ guides, and estimates just over SEK 0.5 billion per year from 2025, with the goal of “one textbook per pupil and subject”.
digital_resilience_e1.context: A government grant that head teachers apply for, covering preschool class, compulsory school, adapted compulsory school, special school and Sami school. The Government argues that basic skills are best developed in analogue environments with analogue tools. Model parameter: national cost level for analogue teaching materials; Kalmar’s share can be scaled by the municipality’s share of the country’s pupils (assumption).

digital_resilience_e14.claim: In 2025, 97% of Swedes (aged 16+) use the internet and 93% use it daily; 3% do not use the internet at all – almost exclusively people of retirement age. 95% use electronic ID.
digital_resilience_e14.context: National survey (Internetstiftelsen, the Swedish Internet Foundation). Practically everyone who lacks electronic ID is 65+. Model parameter: baseline share requiring analogue channels; in Kalmar it should be scaled by the municipality’s share of older people (assumption).

digital_resilience_e17.claim: Assumption: 5% of Kalmar’s adult inhabitants need a fully-fledged analogue channel (in-person visit, telephone, paper) for municipal services in 2026, falling to about 2% by 2050 but never to zero, because new groups (dementia, disability, newly arrived migrants, crisis outages) will always exist.
digital_resilience_e17.context: Derived from 3% non-users in 2025 (e14) and 1.1 million (~11%) under the broad definition in 2018 (e16), plus the fact that almost a quarter have refrained from booking care digitally (e15). Kalmar’s share of older people is roughly on a par with or above the national average (not verified here), hence a value somewhat above 3%. Model assumption; should be calibrated against the municipality’s own statistics.

tech_ai_e5.claim: IEA base case: data centres’ electricity use more than doubles to about 945 TWh in 2030 and about 1,200 TWh in 2035 (range 700–1,700 TWh), with AI as the main driver; emissions rise from 180 to 300 Mt CO2.
tech_ai_e5.context: The range refers to 2035 across sensitivity scenarios. Relevant to Sweden as a host country for data centres (the AI Commission mentions, among other things, Microsoft’s SEK 33.7 billion investment in Swedish data centres). For Kalmar: competition for fossil-free electricity and grid capacity if data centres are established in the region.

tech_ai_e6.claim: AI-based fault location in power grids can shorten outage duration by 30–50%, and AI tools for grid operation can free up as much as 175 GW of transmission capacity globally without new power lines.
tech_ai_e6.context: The IEA’s compilation of applications. The 175 GW figure is global and refers in part to dynamic line rating. Model parameter for the local grid (e.g. Kalmar Energi): fewer outage minutes and more renewables in the existing grid. The actual effect depends on metering data and grid structure.

tech_ai_e9.claim: AI-based flood forecasts achieve equal or better reliability for extreme flows with up to five days’ lead time than the global reference system GloFAS achieves in real time (zero days’ lead time), even in ungauged rivers; the system is used operationally in more than 80 countries.
tech_ai_e9.context: Peer-reviewed in Nature (Google Research et al.). Relevant to climate adaptation for flooding and cloudbursts; for Kalmar mainly coastal high water and cloudbursts, where local data and the models of SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) are crucial. Assumption in the model: earlier warning reduces damage; see also tech_ai_e10.

tech_ai_e12.claim: The AI Commission’s roadmap contains 75 proposals estimated to cost SEK 16,712 million over ten years, of which SEK 11,507 million in the first five years. The Commission notes that smaller government agencies, small regions and municipalities ‘often have not even begun using AI’ and proposes a voluntary AI workshop for the public sector.
tech_ai_e12.context: SOU 2025:12, dated 2025-02-04 in the Riksdag’s document database. Approx. SEK 2.3 billion/year during the first five years. According to the Commission, the proposals do not restrict municipal self-government. National framework for Kalmar’s AI choices.

tech_ai_e14.claim: Public administration spends around SEK 1.5 billion per year on interpreting services; AI-supported interpreting is realistically judged usable in 20–30% of interpreting situations, giving an annual savings potential of SEK 300–450 million. The Swedish National Courts Administration’s AI translation of legal text is estimated to cost 90% less than a translation agency and takes seconds instead of weeks.
tech_ai_e14.context: Range = savings potential in SEK billion/year. Example from SOU 2025:12. Relevant to the inclusion of newly arrived migrants and people with another mother tongue in Kalmar (schools, social services, healthcare). Risk: mistranslation in legal and medical contexts – a human interpreter is needed where mistakes have serious consequences.

tech_ai_e17.claim: Almost 40% of global employment and about 60% of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI; roughly half of the exposed jobs in advanced economies may benefit (productivity), while the rest risk lower labour demand, lower wages and fewer hires.
tech_ai_e17.context: IMF Staff Discussion Note (Cazzaniga et al. 2024), summarised by the head of the IMF. ‘Exposed’ does not mean replaced. Model parameter for a labour-market shock: share of Kalmar’s employed people in exposed occupations × ~50% negative impact (assumption).

tech_ai_e21.claim: Assumption: over 10–20 years, a municipality like Kalmar can realise efficiency gains from AI equivalent to 1–2% of its operating costs, and only if data, skills and governance are in place; without retained manual skills and back-up routines, an AI outage can lead to worse performance than before AI was introduced.
tech_ai_e21.context: Derived from the theoretical ceiling of 5–6% (tech_ai_e13) multiplied by an assumed realisation rate of 20–50%, taking into account that small municipalities often have not started (tech_ai_e12) and the deskilling risk (tech_ai_e3). Model assumption, not measured.

resilience_e3.claim: The new edition of the brochure 'Om krisen eller kriget kommer' (If Crisis or War Comes) was sent out in over 5 million copies to Sweden’s households on 18–29 November 2024, with a stronger focus on war preparedness than the 2018 version.
resilience_e3.context: Shows the state’s national information effort. Can be used as a reference for a municipal campaign (e.g. Kalmar supplementing it with local information about safety points and emergency water).

resilience_e6.claim: The Government is allocating SEK 575 million in the 2026 budget bill to emergency stockpiles, mainly grain and critical inputs for primary production; in September 2025 the Swedish Board of Agriculture was tasked with starting to purchase and store grain.
resilience_e6.context: Decision of 25 September 2025. Shows that food preparedness is being rebuilt nationally after the emergency stockpiles were dismantled following the Cold War. The municipality cannot build state stockpiles itself but can cooperate (e.g. local stocks for large-scale kitchens, agreements with farmers in Kalmar County).

resilience_e8.claim: Kalmar County is at greater risk of water shortage and drought than many other parts of Sweden. On 24 September 2026, groundwater levels in the large aquifers were far below normal throughout the county, all monitored watercourses had flows below mean low flow (MLQ), and watering bans were in force in Mönsterås, Nybro and Vimmerby.
resilience_e8.context: Current situation report from the County Administrative Board. The County Administrative Board estimates that around 180 days of precipitation would be needed for levels in the large aquifers to return to normal across much of the county. The county lies in a rain shadow and precipitation falls mainly in winter. Used to calibrate drought frequency in the model (dry years become more common, not exceptions).

resilience_e9.claim: During the 2016 drought, groundwater levels in south-eastern Sweden (including Kalmar County) were the lowest since measurements began in the 1960s. Mörbylånga was at risk of running out of water; a pipeline from the mainland to Öland was built in three months and could deliver 1,000 m³/day.
resilience_e9.context: SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) describes the 2016 drought (low precipitation since autumn 2015; emergency measures such as pressure reduction, tanker trucks, new pipelines, watering bans). The figure of 1,000 m³/day and Öland’s annual precipitation of 450–550 mm come from Borgholm Energi’s presentation 'Vatten i nöd och kris' (Water in emergencies and crises, 2026). Used as a historical reference event and as an example of the cost/time of emergency water redundancy.

resilience_e10.claim: In Kalmar Municipality, one person is estimated to use about 75 m³ of drinking water per year; inhabitants together use just under 4.8 million m³/year and businesses up to 1 million m³/year. The municipality produces just under 6 million m³ of municipal drinking water per year.
resilience_e10.context: From Kalmar Municipality’s water and sewerage overview (VA-översikt, 2016). 75 m³/year ≈ 205 litres/person/day including the municipality’s share of distribution losses etc. (own conversion; compare with households’ approx. 140 l/day in resilience_e4). Base value for water demand in the model; should be updated with Kalmar Vatten’s current figures.

resilience_e11.claim: Kalmar’s drinking water comes from groundwater in the Nybro esker (Nybroåsen) and from water from the Hagbyån river that is infiltrated into the esker. The estimated maximum abstraction of natural groundwater from the Nybro esker is 5.8 million m³/year, and the separate reserve water sources have a capacity equivalent to 3,400 m³/day.
resilience_e11.context: Same source as resilience_e10. With just under 6 million m³/year (≈16,400 m³/day on average, own conversion), the reserve capacity corresponds to roughly one fifth of normal production – or about 45–50 litres/person/day for 70,000–75,000 inhabitants (own conversion), i.e. above the Swedish Food Agency’s emergency water levels but far below normal consumption. Natural abstraction from the Nybro esker (5.8 Mm³) is close to current production, which makes artificial infiltration and recycled water crucial for growth.

resilience_e12.claim: Kalmar Vatten AB is building a new resource recovery plant (kretsloppsverk; investment decision 2022, planned operation 2026/2027) which, in addition to wastewater treatment, will produce recycled water for uses including drinking water production, irrigation and industry, as well as biogas and biofertiliser. Discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus to Kalmar Strait are expected to fall by at least 35% compared with the current treatment plant.
resilience_e12.context: From Kalmar Municipality’s Water Services Plan (Vattentjänstplan; consultation document, undated; published in the EuroBalt project’s document archive 2026). The resource recovery plant is Kalmar’s most important existing measure for both water security (reuse) and the Baltic Sea. The volume of recycled water is not stated in the document – it must be obtained from Kalmar Vatten.

resilience_e13.claim: Borgholm Energi’s desalination plant in Sandvik (Öland, inaugurated 2017) produces 3,000 m³ of fresh water per day from 6,000 m³ of seawater (half is returned as saltier brine). The plant cost SEK 85 million plus SEK 28 million for pipelines; the water and sewerage tariff was raised by 5.3%.
resilience_e13.context: Provides a cost parameter: about SEK 28,000 of investment per m³/day of capacity for the plant (own calculation: SEK 85 million / 3,000), excluding pipelines and operation. Gotland’s desalination plant (since 2019) has a capacity of 7,500 m³/day but has had shutdowns due to algae (SVT 2025) – desalination is not problem-free in the Baltic Sea.

resilience_e14.claim: Seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) typically uses 3.5–4.5 kWh of electricity per m³ of water produced; the range in the literature is 3–6.7 kWh/m³ depending on the raw water, quality requirements and plant efficiency.
resilience_e14.context: Applies to ocean seawater (~35 per mille salt). Used to link water security to the energy system: 3,000 m³/day × 4 kWh ≈ 12 MWh/day. Globally, in 2019, about 95 million m³ of desalinated water and 142 million m³ of brine were produced per day (Jones et al. 2019, Science of the Total Environment) – brine is an environmental issue in Kalmar Strait too.

resilience_e15.claim: Assumption: desalinating brackish water from Kalmar Strait requires about 1.5–2.5 kWh/m³, i.e. roughly half as much as ocean seawater.
resilience_e15.context: Model assumption. Reasoning: the energy demand of reverse osmosis increases with salinity (Kim et al. 2019, Applied Energy: 'high salinity increases energy demand'), and the Baltic Proper has a much lower salinity than the world’s oceans. However, pumping, pre-treatment (algae, see resilience_e13) and brine management make up a fixed share of the energy, so we do not scale linearly. Should be replaced with a measured value from Borgholm Energi or Region Gotland.

resilience_e16.claim: Mean sea level in Kalmar is projected (SSP5-8.5, median) to rise from 12 cm (2022) to 35 cm (2050), 82 cm (2100), 97 cm (2120) and 126 cm (2150) in the RH2000 height system. Likely range in 2120: 63–142 cm.
resilience_e16.context: Municipality-level data from SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) (2022), taking local land uplift into account, compiled in a flood study for a detailed development plan in Kalmar Municipality. 2120 is the closest year to the game’s final year, 2126. For lower emissions scenarios the rise is smaller (see resilience_e19). Used as an exogenous driver of flood risk.

resilience_e17.claim: A 100-year high water level in Kalmar is currently (2022) about 130 cm RH2000 and is projected (SSP5-8.5) to reach 200 cm in 2100, 215 cm in 2120 and 244 cm in 2150. The calculated highest water level in 2120 is 252 cm (218–297).
resilience_e17.context: Return values for Kalmar from SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) (2018) added to future mean sea level (SMHI 2022). Kalmar’s planning level of +2.8 m corresponds to the upper percentile of a 200-year high water level in 2120 plus a 0.15 m margin. Used to calculate how much of Kvarnholmen, Ängö, Varvsholmen and other low-lying areas is flooded during extreme events per decade.

resilience_e18.claim: Kalmar Municipality requires new buildings to withstand flood water up to +2.8 m (RH2000). The municipality’s worst-case scenario is about 1.1 m of sea level rise by 2100 plus temporary rises of a further 1.5 m. The city of Kalmar is one of 25 areas in Sweden that the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency (MSB) has assessed as having a significant flood risk. Detailed cost estimates for adaptation are not yet available.
resilience_e18.context: From the climate adaptation section of the comprehensive plan. The municipality describes four strategies: adapt (e.g. houses on stilts, floodable ground floors), protect (embankments, walls), 'attack' (move the shoreline outwards through land reclamation) and relocate (abandon and move to higher ground). The County Administrative Board recommends 2.7 m in the northern part of the county and 2.8 m in the southern part and on Öland (SVT 2018). Vital societal functions: 400-year flow + 0.5 m margin.

resilience_e19.claim: IPCC AR6: global mean sea level is projected to rise by 28–55 cm by 2100 under very low emissions (SSP1-1.9), 44–76 cm under intermediate emissions (SSP2-4.5) and 63–101 cm under very high emissions (SSP5-8.5), relative to 1995–2014.
resilience_e19.context: How much the sea is perceived to rise locally depends on land uplift, which is small in the Kalmar area compared with northern Sweden. The game’s climate choice (global emissions scenario) should determine which curve Kalmar follows; resilience_e16 is the high scenario.

resilience_e22.claim: Assumption: the starting value for the share of Kalmar households that can manage 7 days without help from society (both food and water) is set at 0.35 (35%). A municipal preparedness campaign raises the share by at most 10–15 percentage points per decade.
resilience_e22.context: Calibrated against the Swedish Food Agency’s 2025 population survey (resilience_e23): 61% have food for a week but only 36% have enough to drink for a week. The share that manages both is therefore probably at most about 36%. Residents of Småland and the islands (Småland med öarna), the region that includes Kalmar County, say more often than average that they can cook food and boil water without electricity. This points to a value close to, or slightly above, the national average. The recommendation (resilience_e1) and the brochure (resilience_e3) have reached all households, but stockpiling requires money and space. Socio-economic differences should therefore be modelled, with a lower share among tenants, younger people and economically vulnerable groups.

biodiversity_baltic_e3.claim: The Planetary Health Check 2025 (Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, PIK) assesses that seven of nine planetary boundaries have been transgressed; ocean acidification is the seventh boundary to be crossed.
biodiversity_baltic_e3.context: Annual report. Shows the trend of 3 → 6 → 7 transgressed boundaries over 2009–2025. In the game, Kalmar’s share (per capita footprint) can be compared against these global boundaries.

biodiversity_baltic_e4.claim: Over 96% of the Baltic Sea area is not in good status with regard to eutrophication, including the entire open sea and 86% of coastal waters (HELCOM assessment 2011–2016), despite a slight long-term improvement.
biodiversity_baltic_e4.context: From HELCOM’s updated Baltic Sea Action Plan (BSAP 2021, adopted in Lübeck on 20 October 2021, measures to be implemented by 2030). Status has recently deteriorated in four of 17 sub-basins. Starting value for the indicator 'eutrophication status of Kalmar Strait'.

biodiversity_baltic_e5.claim: To achieve good status with regard to eutrophication, inputs to the Baltic Sea may not exceed 792,209 tonnes of nitrogen and 21,716 tonnes of phosphorus per year (maximum allowable inputs, MAI). For the Baltic Proper, to which Kalmar Strait belongs, the ceiling is 325,000 tonnes of nitrogen and 7,360 tonnes of phosphorus per year.
biodiversity_baltic_e5.context: HELCOM BSAP 2021, table 1. Used as the ecological ceiling for nutrient load in the game’s doughnut. Airborne nitrogen accounts for 27% of the total nitrogen load; diffuse sources (mainly agriculture) dominate riverine inputs.

biodiversity_baltic_e6.claim: Sweden’s net input ceiling (NIC) for inputs to the Baltic Proper is 30,690 tonnes of nitrogen and 318 tonnes of phosphorus per year. All measures required to meet the ceilings must be fully implemented by 2027.
biodiversity_baltic_e6.context: HELCOM BSAP 2021, tables 2a/2b. Kalmar Municipality’s share can be scaled in the model by catchment area or population (an assumption that should be replaced with data from VISS/SMED). Provides a concrete 'budget' for the game’s nitrogen indicator.

biodiversity_baltic_e8.claim: Along the Swedish Baltic coast, a regime shift has taken place from dominance by large predatory fish (perch, pike) to three-spined stickleback. Fish surveys in 486 shallow bays along 1,200 km of coastline in 1979–2017 show that the shift began in the outer archipelago and has gradually spread towards the mainland coast; sticklebacks eat the predators’ fry, which reinforces the shift.
biodiversity_baltic_e8.context: Eklöf et al. 2020 (Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, SLU, and others). The study area covers the Swedish east coast including Kalmar County. Shows that coastal ecosystems can 'tip' locally and that the shift can spread – justifies measures for predatory fish (spawning grounds, fishing rules) in Kalmar Strait. Seals and cormorants are discussed in the literature as contributing factors but are not included in this summary.

biodiversity_baltic_e9.claim: In July 2019 the EU introduced emergency measures (Implementing Regulation 2019/1248) banning targeted fishing for eastern Baltic cod in subdivisions 24–26, because the stock had unsustainably low biomass due to weak recruitment, environmental factors, high natural mortality and excessive fishing.
biodiversity_baltic_e9.context: Targeted cod fishing has since been closed in practice. Shows that the economic base of fishing in Kalmar Strait cannot be taken for granted – ecosystem recovery is a prerequisite. The source is an environmental organisation’s summary of the regulation.

biodiversity_baltic_e10.claim: In the 2025 Red List (Rödlista 2025), 23,103 species in Sweden were assessed; 5,217 (nearly 23%) are red-listed and 2,373 (10%) are threatened. The number of red-listed species has increased by 10% since 2020 (from 4,746). The factors affecting the most red-listed species are overgrowth on land and a lack of continuity forest, followed by fishing (e.g. bottom trawling), land development, drainage of wetlands and climate change.
biodiversity_baltic_e10.context: Published on 24 March 2026 by the SLU Swedish Species Information Centre (SLU Artdatabanken; report 37). The increase is partly due to better knowledge. The agricultural landscape (7,641 assessed species) is crucial – overgrowth when grazing ends affects Öland’s alvar and Kalmar County’s wooded pastures. The otter and the white-tailed eagle left the list thanks to growing populations – measures work.

biodiversity_baltic_e14.claim: In the plains of southern Sweden, an estimated 80–90% of the original wetlands have disappeared through drainage since the 19th century.
biodiversity_baltic_e14.context: The figure is often cited with reference to the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency, but has only been verified here in secondary sources (material from environmental organisations). Borgholm Energi describes Öland as 'heavily drained'. Use it as an order of magnitude for restoration potential, not as an exact value.

biodiversity_baltic_e15.claim: The EU Nature Restoration Regulation (EU 2024/1991, in force 18 August 2024) requires restoration measures on at least 20% of the EU’s land and sea areas by 2030 and on all ecosystems in need of restoration by 2050. Among other things, it requires no net loss of urban green space and tree cover by 2030, that the decline of pollinators be reversed by 2030, and that at least 25,000 km of rivers be restored to free-flowing rivers. National restoration plans must be submitted by September 2026.
biodiversity_baltic_e15.context: A legally binding framework that affects Kalmar’s planning (urban greenery, wetlands, watercourses). In the game: a floor level that cannot be opted out of after 2030.

biodiversity_baltic_e16.claim: The Agricultural Landscape of Southern Öland became a World Heritage Site in 2000 and covers 56,323 hectares; Stora Alvaret makes up about half of the World Heritage Site and about a quarter of Öland’s area, and is Europe’s largest limestone pavement of its kind, with many rare species.
biodiversity_baltic_e16.context: The alvar depends on continued grazing; overgrowth is the greatest threat to red-listed species (biodiversity_baltic_e10). The source is Wikipedia (UNESCO’s page could not be retrieved) – should be double-checked against whc.unesco.org/en/list/968.

biodiversity_baltic_e17.claim: Kalmar County has more irrigation ponds and constructed wetlands than the national average, especially on Öland, as well as several desalination plants and water reuse systems. The County Administrative Board, the Rural Economy and Agricultural Society (Hushållningssällskapet) and LRF Sydost (Federation of Swedish Farmers, South-East) share the vision that 'not a single drop should go to waste'.
biodiversity_baltic_e17.context: Opinion piece/news item from the County Administrative Board, 8 July 2026. Shows that wetlands in Kalmar already serve a dual function: water storage for agriculture (resilience) and nutrient trap (the Baltic Sea). The starting value for wetland area should be taken from the County Administrative Board’s LOVA/LONA statistics (local water and nature conservation grants).

biodiversity_baltic_e18.claim: Assumption: a new agricultural wetland in Kalmar’s catchments (Hagbyån, Ljungbyån and others) removes an average of 200 kg of nitrogen and 5 kg of phosphorus per hectare per year.
biodiversity_baltic_e18.context: Model assumption. Reasoning: Land et al. (2016) show a median of 930 kg N/ha/year but that removal is strongly load-dependent; agricultural runoff in south-eastern Sweden has lower loading than wastewater, low precipitation (450–550 mm on Öland) and dry summers when flow stops. We therefore set about one fifth of the median. Phosphorus: Land et al. found lower P efficiency for wetlands on former arable land. Should be calibrated against Swedish follow-up studies (Swedish Board of Agriculture/SLU).

biodiversity_baltic_e19.claim: Assumption: the eutrophication status of Kalmar Strait responds to reduced nutrient inputs with a delay of 20–40 years.
biodiversity_baltic_e19.context: Model assumption based on HELCOM’s observation that the Baltic Sea, which has been subject to human pressure for over a century and has accumulated nutrients in its sediments, 'may need several decades to fully recover even after a significant reduction in inputs' (BSAP 2021). In the game, this means that decisions taken in the 2020s become visible only around 2050–2070 – a central teaching point about the generational perspective.

governance_e3.claim: Ten years after its adoption, the Act has gained greater prominence but is not driving the system-wide change that was intended, according to Wales’s public audit body (Audit Wales, April 2025).
governance_e3.context: The report “No time to lose” found good examples but also bodies that had given the Act no explicit consideration; health care lagged behind. Recommendations: reduce financial uncertainty, invest in prevention, review monitoring. Model parameter: a future generations law without a link to the budget should have a weak effect (assumption), a lesson for a Kalmar version.

governance_e6.claim: None of just over 150 countries studied meets its inhabitants’ basic needs at a level of resource use that would be globally sustainable.
governance_e6.context: O’Neill et al. downscaled planetary boundaries to per capita level and compared them with social thresholds. Physical needs (nutrition, sanitation, electricity, eliminating extreme poverty) can probably be met for everyone within the boundaries, but more ambitious social goals currently require unsustainable resource use. Indicates that a “doughnut portrait” of Kalmar is likely to show red segments in the ceiling.

governance_e8.claim: On 8 April 2020, Amsterdam adopted a circular strategy based on the Doughnut model, aiming to halve the use of new raw materials by 2030 and to be fully circular by 2050.
governance_e8.context: Kate Raworth and the Doughnut Economics Action Lab (DEAL) produced the “Amsterdam City Doughnut” as a basis. The city ran about 200 projects (sharing, repair, reuse). These are targets, not results achieved – the outcome for 2030 is not yet known. A model for a Kalmar doughnut.

governance_e12.claim: The target level for 1.5-degree lifestyles in 2050 is 0.7 t CO2e per person per year (1.4 t in 2040).
governance_e12.context: Same source as governance_e11; the project website, which presents the 2025 update “A Climate for Sufficiency”, gives the same target levels. The Swedish Environmental Protection Agency gives a rough guideline of no more than 1 t CO2e per person per year globally by 2050. Game parameter: target pathway 2.5 → 1.4 → 0.7 t for Kalmar’s inhabitants.

governance_e14.claim: According to SEI’s Konsumtionskompassen (Consumption Compass, developed with Kalmar and Umeå municipalities), household consumption emissions were 5.4 t CO2e per person in 2023; including public consumption (0.83 t) and investment (2.09 t), the total is about 8.3 t. Transport accounts for 37%, food about 20% and housing 14% of the household share.
governance_e14.context: The difference from the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency’s 7.6 t is due to methodology. Emissions per person differ little between groups of municipalities but a great deal between households (income, geography, type of housing). The breakdown (transport 37%, food ~20–21%, housing 14%, leisure 8%) can be used to weight the game’s measures. Funded by Formas (ref. no. 2022-02014).

governance_e16.claim: Kalmar Municipality aims to be climate neutral as early as 2030 (no net emissions, equivalent to an 85% reduction compared with 1990) and is one of 23 municipalities in Viable Cities’ Climate City Contract 2030.
governance_e16.context: The target covers the entire geographical area. Since 2019, Kalmar has had a target of being a fossil-fuel-free municipality by 2030; the climate contract (January 2023) raised the ambition. Kalmar.se confirms the target “Kalmar shall be climate neutral by 2030”. The target year is 15 years ahead of Sweden’s 2045 target – a contrast the game can use.

governance_e17.claim: According to the municipality, Kalmar’s greenhouse gas emissions have fallen from 7.9 to 3.6 tonnes per person per year; 58% of energy use comes from renewable sources and 41% of the debt portfolio consists of green loans.
governance_e17.context: The municipality’s own summary; the base year and method are not stated on the page (probably territorial emissions, not consumption-based). It should therefore not be compared directly with the consumption-based 7.6–8.3 t. Starting value for the game’s territorial climate indicator for Kalmar.

governance_e18.claim: Kalmar’s carbon budget (Paris Agreement) is about 1.4 million tonnes of fossil CO2 from 2022; at 2022 emission levels (about 180,000 tonnes) it will run out within seven years, and emissions need to fall by 12.9% per year from 2023.
governance_e18.context: Calculated by Klimatsekretariatet with Uppsala University (the same model is used by many municipalities). Covers territorial fossil CO2 plus international aviation and shipping allocated per capita. About 1.2 Mt remained in 2023. Directly usable as the annual reduction rate in the game’s climate module for Kalmar.

governance_e19.claim: Kalmar’s longest official planning horizon is 2050: the comprehensive plan runs to 2035 with an outlook to 2050, the vision extends to 2035, and the budget covers one year plus a plan for two more years.
governance_e19.context: “Kalmar kommuns översiktsplan 2035 med utblick mot 2050” (Kalmar Municipality’s comprehensive plan 2035 with an outlook to 2050) was adopted by the municipal council on 19 June 2023 and became legally binding on 30 May 2025 after an appeal (https://kalmar.se/arkiv/nyhetsarkiv/nyheter/2025-06-05-kommunfullmaktiges-beslut-att-anta-oversiktsplanen-har-fatt-laga-kraft.html). Vision 2035 (“Tillsammans gör vi ett Kalmar för alla ännu bättre…”, “Together we make a Kalmar for everyone even better…”) is published on kalmar.se. The budget is set for the coming year with a plan for the following two years (the Local Government Act’s requirement for a three-year plan). Counting from 2026, the horizon is therefore 9 years (vision), 24 years (comprehensive plan outlook) and 3 years (finances) – a long way from 100 years.

demography_e9.claim: Kalmar Municipality grew from 59,308 inhabitants in 2000 to 72,704 in 2024 (+22.6%, about 0.85% per year), faster than Kalmar County, which largely stood still (235,391 → 246,352).
demography_e9.context: Statistics Sweden (SCB) table BefolkningNy, retrieved via the API on 2026-10-08. Over the same period, Sweden as a whole grew from 8.88 to 10.59 million. In 2024 the share aged 80+ was 6.0% in Kalmar Municipality, 7.9% in the county and 6.1% nationally. Starting values for the game (2026).

demography_e10.claim: The Statistics Sweden (SCB) regional projection gives Kalmar Municipality 75,100 inhabitants in 2030, 80,200 in 2050 and 83,600 in 2070 (about +0.30% per year); the share aged 80+ rises from 6.1% to 11.0% and the old-age dependency ratio from 36 to 50.
demography_e10.context: Table BefProgRegFakN (regional projection 2024–2070), our own aggregation: 72,774 (2024), 75,138 (2030), 78,079 (2040), 80,239 (2050), 83,609 (2070). Share aged 0–19: 22.7% → 19.9%. Old-age dependency ratio (65+/20–64): 35.9 (2024) → 43.0 (2050) → 49.8 (2070). Regional projections are more uncertain than national ones (migration patterns). Baseline pathway for the game up to 2070.

demography_e11.claim: Kalmar County is projected to have a largely unchanged population (246,500 in 2024, 249,000 in 2070) but to age sharply: the share aged 80+ rises from 7.9% to 13.0% and the old-age dependency ratio from 50 to 63.
demography_e11.context: Same table as demography_e10. The county passes through a dip around 2040 (243,000). Kalmar Municipality is the county’s engine of growth, while many smaller municipalities are ageing faster – relevant for regional cooperation, commuting and the sizing of health care.

demography_e13.claim: In 2025, 42.0% of Sweden’s households were single-person households (44.7% in Kalmar Municipality), while “other households” – which include multigenerational households, among others – made up 8.1% nationally and 5.6% in Kalmar.
demography_e13.context: Statistics Sweden (SCB) table HushallT22 (retrieved via the API on 2026-10-08), our own calculation. “Other households” covers households that are not single people or cohabiting couples with or without children, e.g. adult children living with parents, several generations or friends sharing a home – the share is therefore an upper limit for multigenerational living. Single people aged 65+ make up 16.9% of all households nationally (16.7% in Kalmar). Kalmar has 35,876 households.

demography_e18.claim: Assumption: Kalmar Municipality has about 96,000 inhabitants in 2126 (range 84,000–110,000), and 13–14% of its inhabitants are aged 80 or over.
demography_e18.context: No official municipal projection exists beyond 2070. Reasoning: the Statistics Sweden (SCB) regional pathway for Kalmar (+0.30%/year 2024–2070, demography_e10) is slightly above the national one (+0.24%/year). The national database extension grows +0.19%/year 2070–2120 (demography_e2). We assume +0.25%/year 2070–2126: 83,600 × 1.0025^56 ≈ 96,000. Lower bound: zero growth after 2070 (≈ 84,000); upper bound: +0.5%/year (≈ 110,000), i.e. roughly half the rate of 2000–2024. The share aged 80+ follows the national pathway (11.3% in 2070 → 13.6% in 2120) at Kalmar’s slightly lower level. To be varied with the player’s choices (housing, migration, fertility).

food.summary: How much land a population needs depends more on what it eats than on how it farms: land requirements per person differ by up to eight times between diets, and the average Swedish diet exceeds the global per-capita boundaries for climate, cropland and nutrients by two to four times. Kalmar County is one of Sweden's most agriculture-intensive counties, with roughly twice as much arable land per inhabitant as Sweden as a whole and the country's largest share of pasture, while Kalmar Municipality is roughly at the national average and has a shrinking horticulture sector. Urban growing gives high yields per square metre, but mainly vegetables and social value; the calories must come from the surrounding farmland, so self-sufficiency is a regional question rather than an urban one. Diets in public meals, protection of arable land, emergency stockpiles and cooperation with the county's farmers are the municipality's strongest levers, while mussel farming in Kalmar Strait is an interesting but expensive complement for nutrient removal in the brackish water of the Baltic Sea.

energy.summary: Kalmar has good conditions for renewable energy: solar PV produces around 1,000 kWh per installed kWp per year on a south-facing roof, and the county already has some of the highest solar capacity per inhabitant in the country. The biofuel-fired Moskogen combined heat and power plant covers about 90 per cent of district heating demand and a third of the municipality's electricity demand, but solar power is highly seasonal and requires storage, flexibility and supplementary wind or biopower in winter. Offshore wind in the southern Baltic Sea has great potential, but in 2024 the Government rejected thirteen wind farms on defence grounds, which makes local generation, energy communities and energy efficiency all the more important. The costs of solar, onshore wind and batteries have fallen sharply since 2010, while Sweden's electricity demand is expected to more than double by 2045, creating competition for electricity, land and grid capacity.

mobility.summary: In Kalmar Municipality the car currently accounts for about 60% of passenger transport, and 44% of car trips in the urban area are shorter than five kilometres – a large potential for walking, cycling and e-bikes. Research shows clear health benefits of active travel (cycle commuting is linked to markedly lower mortality) and that urban environments with less car traffic, such as Barcelona's superblocks, can prevent hundreds of premature deaths per year in a large city. Experience from Pontevedra, Oslo and Ghent shows that car-free or low-car centres are possible, but the effects on retail and accessibility must be actively managed, especially for older people, people with disabilities and commuters from rural areas. Blue-green solutions and de-paving can at the same time reduce stormwater flows and flood damage, which is important for a coastal Kalmar facing more frequent cloudbursts.

community.summary: Social relationships are as strong a survival factor as well-known risk factors: meta-analyses show a 50% higher likelihood of survival for people with strong social ties, and the WHO links loneliness to about 871,000 deaths a year worldwide. In Sweden, 7–8% of adults have no close friend, a quarter are troubled by loneliness and 41% of households consist of one person – figures that are particularly relevant for Kalmar County, where 26% are aged 65 or over. The municipality can influence this through social infrastructure (libraries, meeting places, green spaces, activities in residential care homes), community and intergenerational housing, deliberative democracy (citizens' assemblies, participatory budgeting) and working-time trials that free up time for relationships and civic engagement. The evidence is strong for the link between loneliness and health but weaker and more context-dependent for the effect of individual measures, which the model should reflect with cautious effect sizes.

health.summary: Life expectancy in Kalmar is on a par with Sweden as a whole (men 81.8 years, women 85.9 years in 2021–2025), but the county has an older population than the country (26% are 65+), which increases pressure on health and social care and on dementia care – dementia already costs society SEK 90–100 billion a year. Strong evidence shows that nature and greenery close to home (at least 120 minutes in nature a week, a green space within 300 metres) and physical activity (150–300 minutes a week) prevent both physical and mental ill-health, and that preventive public health measures on average return several kronor for every krona invested. At the same time, psychosomatic complaints among young people are rising – 77% of 15-year-old girls have recurring complaints – and only one in five schoolchildren is sufficiently active. Kalmar is well placed, with the coast, forests and Kalmar Strait close at hand, but urban densification risks eating into green spaces.

digital_resilience.summary: Since 2023, Sweden has swung from “digital first” in schools to analogue teaching materials, a phone-free school day (law from 1 August 2026) and national screen-time recommendations for children. At the same time, the state is building up analogue back-up capacity in the payment system: legal requirements that grocery stores and pharmacies accept cash and offline card payments for essential goods for up to seven days apply from 1 July 2026. The evidence on screen and phone restrictions is mixed – some studies show improved results for low-performing pupils and girls, others no effect on well-being. For Kalmar, the question is which functions should have an analogue back-up (schools, payments, information, municipal services) and how to avoid shutting out the roughly 3% who do not use the internet – mostly older people. A coastal municipality with many older residents and a location close to the security-policy tensions around the Baltic Sea has particular reasons to plan for outages in electricity, telecoms and payments.

tech_ai.summary: The evidence points to a few areas where AI delivers large, documented public benefit: a Swedish randomised trial (MASAI) shows that AI-supported mammography finds 29% more cancers with a 44% lower reading workload, AI can shorten power outages by 30–50% and give flood warnings several days earlier, and AI-supported interpreting can sharply reduce costs in the public sector. At the same time there are clear risks: data centres’ electricity demand is expected to more than double by 2030, professional skills can erode (endoscopists detected fewer polyps after getting used to AI), and surveillance is restricted only by the EU AI Act. The AI Commission’s roadmap (SOU 2025:12) proposes 75 measures costing just under SEK 17 billion over ten years and notes that many smaller municipalities have not even begun using AI. For Kalmar, the choice is about where to accelerate (healthcare together with the region, the energy system, language support, preparedness) and which guardrails – transparency, sovereignty, retained human expertise – are needed.

resilience.summary: Sweden’s total defence planning assumes that society must be able to cope with at least three months of a security policy crisis, including war, and households are urged by the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency (MCF, formerly the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency, MSB) to manage on their own for at least one week. The security situation in the Baltic Sea has become more tense since Sweden joined NATO in 2024 and since several undersea cables and gas pipelines were damaged in 2023–2024. For Kalmar, water is the most tangible vulnerability: Kalmar County is one of the driest areas in Sweden, groundwater was at a record low in 2016 and in September 2026 is once again far below normal, and Öland has had to build a pipeline from the mainland and desalination plants. At the same time, calculations based on data from SMHI (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute) indicate that mean sea level in Kalmar could rise by around one metre by 2120 in a high-emissions scenario, and the city of Kalmar is one of 25 areas in Sweden with a significant flood risk. Preparedness in the game is therefore about both war/crisis (days of self-sufficiency) and slow-onset climate risks (water, sea level).

biodiversity_baltic.summary: According to the latest Planetary Health Check (2025), humanity has transgressed seven of nine planetary boundaries, including biosphere integrity and nitrogen and phosphorus flows – the two boundaries most clearly visible off Kalmar’s shores. Over 96% of the Baltic Sea is not in good status with regard to eutrophication, oxygen-free seabeds have increased tenfold in a century, the eastern Baltic cod stock has collapsed, and along the Swedish coast the three-spined stickleback has taken over from perch and pike in more and more bays. In Sweden, 23% of the assessed species are red-listed (2025), mainly because of overgrowth when grazing ends and a lack of old-growth forest – threats that are highly relevant to Öland’s alvar and Kalmar County’s agricultural landscape. There are proven measures with known effects: wetlands, catch crops, better wastewater treatment and protected areas, but the Baltic Sea responds with a delay of decades.

governance.summary: Long-term governance is about giving future generations a voice in today’s decisions. The Welsh Well-being of Future Generations Act (2015) and Finland’s Committee for the Future (since 1993) show that long-term thinking can be institutionalised, but evaluations show that the effect depends on whether it is tied to budgets and investment. The Doughnut model (Raworth 2017) and the Stockholm Resilience Centre’s “wedding cake” provide frameworks for a good life within planetary boundaries, and Amsterdam and Tomelilla already use them in their governance. Kalmar has an ambitious climate target (climate neutral by 2030), but its vision extends only to 2035 and the comprehensive plan looks ahead to 2050 – we have not found any Swedish municipality with a formally adopted hundred-year vision (limited search). In the game, the player can build the institutions for responsibility towards the future that are missing today.

demography.summary: Sweden is growing slowly and ageing: the Statistics Sweden (SCB) projection gives 11.8 million inhabitants in 2070 and – in the statistical database’s extension – just under 13 million in 2120, driven almost entirely by immigration because more people die than are born. Fertility is at a record low (1.43 children per woman in 2024 and 2025), and the share of people aged 80 and over is expected to almost double by 2070. Kalmar Municipality has grown faster than Sweden as a whole and is projected to reach just under 84,000 inhabitants in 2070, while Kalmar County as a whole is standing still and ageing sharply. Swedes unusually often live alone and leave home early, so multigenerational living would be a real cultural change. There are no official municipal projections beyond 2070 – the game’s values for 2070–2126 are explicit assumptions.
